headlines.title: New video shows Eric Swalwell's stop by federal agents at SFO
headlines.description: Newly released surveillance video shows former East Bay Congressman Eric Swalwell being approached and escorted through San Francisco International Airport by federal agents. The footage was released by airport authorities in response to a public records request by NBC Bay Area’s Investigative Unit. The video appears to show federal agents approaching and surrounding Swalwell near the gate shortly after his arrival to San Francisco’s International Airport on Aug. 15. Swalwell, who is seen wearing a black hoodie sweater and baseball hat, appears to cooperate as he hands what looks like his cellphone to a female agent. He is seen carrying a backpack and rolling suitcase as the agents escort him through the airport, up an escalator and into a restricted area. Court records show federal agents executed a search warrant at SFO at approximately 8:25 p.m. The property inventory identifies the seized items as a white Apple iPhone, a charging cable and adapter, and an Apple MacBook Pro. The following day, federal agents searched Swalwell’s Washington, D.C., residence. He has not been charged with a crime. California Aug 20 Congress Apr 13 Publicly available warrant records cite a federal civil rights statute, Title 18, Section 242, which makes it a crime for someone acting under government authority to willfully deprive another person of federally protected rights. Multiple women have accused the former congressman of misconduct, including sexual assault and sending unsolicited explicit messages. Swalwell has denied the allegations, describing them through his attorney as false and politically motivated. Swalwell resigned from Congress and ended his campaign for California governor in April after the allegations became public. Before his resignation, the House Ethics Committee had announced its own investigation, while emphasizing that opening an inquiry did not mean a violation had occurred. The FBI previously declined to comment on the circumstances surrounding the airport encounter. Swalwell and his attorneys have not addressed the incident.

headlines.title: Apple's new CEO, John Ternus, takes over from Tim Cook after 15 years
headlines.description: Apple’s new CEO John Ternus takes the helm of the iconic tech giant on Tuesday, ending Tim Cook’s 15-year tenure during which the company’s value skyrocketed to $4.6 trillion thanks to the iPhone’s enormous popularity. The transition to a new CEO comes at a pivotal time for Apple. Artificial intelligence has unleashed the greatest upheaval within the industry since Steve Jobs unveiled the first iPhone in 2007. Apple has gotten off to a rough start in AI after stumbling in its efforts to deliver new features built on the technology, as promised nearly two years ago. Earlier this year, it unveiled new artificial intelligence advances, including upgrades to its Siri assistant, emphasizing a focus on privacy and day-to-day use as the iPhone maker tries to catch up with rivals. Ternus faces challenges that will force him to step outside his comfort zone in hardware engineering. Beyond finding ways to keep Apple competitive in the artificial intelligence race, he will need to navigate supply chain questions and relationships with figures such as President Donald Trump, who offered public praise for his predecessor on Tuesday. Serving as Apple CEO will also require soft skills, including developing relationships with important figures. Cook cultivated ties with Trump as he navigated the company through business challenges, including Trump’s trade and tariff war targeting countries in Asia, where Apple has extensive manufacturing supply chains. Although he is handing over the CEO reins at Apple, Cook is widely expected to help the company maintain a good relationship with Trump after he shifts to his new role as executive chairman. Ternus worked on some of Apple’s signature products under Cook, including the Apple Watch, AirPods and Apple Vision Pro. He will headline next week’s launch of the latest iPhone at Apple’s Cupertino, California, headquarters.
headlines.source: The Associated Press | The Associated Press

headlines.title: Overturned vehicle closes I-80 off-ramps to Treasure Island
headlines.description: An overturned vehicle on Interstate 80 is closing access to Treasure Island Road from both directions, according to the California Highway Patrol. The crash prompted the closure of the eastbound and westbound I-80 off-ramps to Treasure Island and Yerba Buena Island. The off-ramps are estimated to reopen around 2 p.m. Motorists should expect delays in the area. No information about possible injuries was immediately available. This is a developing story. Please check back for updates. This story uses functionality that may not work in our app. Click here to open the story in your web browser.

headlines.title: Prolific South Bay burglar busted again on suspicion of burglary
headlines.description: A man who was convicted of dozens of burglaries in San Jose was arrested on suspicion of more of them, police said Monday. On Aug. 17 just before 5 a.m., officers responded to a report of vandalism of a business in the 3100 block of Senter Road. Investigators found that a man threw a brick through the front door of a business, “causing thousands worth in damages,” the department said. The suspect fled the scene before police arrived. Detectives identified Jonny Miles, 42, as the suspect in that case. Investigators later linked Miles to an attempted burglary on Aug. 18 on East Capitol Expressway, where a rock was again thrown at a door that was then kicked down. The suspect fled the scene. According to police, Miles was arrested in July, allegedly mid-burglary, on suspicion of three other burglaries. He was again arrested on Aug. 20 in San Jose on suspicion of burglary. Miles was charged with 15 commercial burglaries in Santa Clara County in 2020, for which he served about two years in jail, according to police. After being released in 2023, he was then charged with 23 more burglaries and went back to jail until May of this year. Miles was in custody as of Monday, being held on suspicion of burglary.

headlines.title: Social media companies are trying harder to know which users are kids
headlines.description: Of the child safety measures agreed to in Meta’s landmark legal settlement, no category contains more detailed requirements than its commitments on age assurance — and for good reason. No matter how well the protections work, they are of little use if Meta can’t tell which users are kids. Determining which accounts belong to children is also the linchpin of child safety measures that other companies, including Google, TikTok, and Roblox, are ramping up as public and regulatory sentiment turns against them in the U.S. and other countries. The Meta settlement — with protections the company says could become industry standards — will give the social media giant a year to refine its approach. But the options are limited, and improving age verification technology presents steep challenges, including navigating privacy implications not just for children but for adults who could have to prove they are over 18. The $18 billion settlement resolves claims from state attorneys general that it hurt children’s mental health by deliberately designing its Instagram and Facebook platforms in ways that hooked young people’s attention. The agreement announced last week with the Menlo Park, California, company involves 48 states plus the District of Columbia and U.S. territories. Tech companies lean on AI for estimating ages In the offline world, people use government-issued IDs to prove they are over 18 or 21, whether they want to get into a club or buy cigarettes. While this technically works online too, many people are not comfortable giving a Big Tech company like Meta or Google access to their driver’s license or passport. Meta accepts IDs to check ages, and promises to delete them within 30 days. Beyond IDs, though, a growing number of tech companies are using artificial intelligence to try to determine users’ ages. This is not true age verification. While AI can estimate a person’s age, often accurately, it can’t verify a person’s birth date. Last year, Google began using an age-assurance system for YouTube that relies on AI to differentiate between adults and minors based on their watch histories. Meta does the same. AI age checks use clues to determine how old someone is. On Instagram, this includes “contextual clues” such as posts about birthday celebrations or school, and things like which posts people like, comment or linger on, who their friends are, as well as the times of day they log in. For instance, someone who is offline during school hours would likely be school-aged. In a blog post last year, Meta said its AI also looks at photos people post for visual cues, including “height or bone structure, to estimate someone’s general age; it does not identify the specific person in the image.” “By combining these visual insights with our analysis of text and interactions, we can significantly increase the number of underage accounts we identify and remove,” the company added. Under the settlement, Meta agreed to strengthen its age-checking technology using its own tools, as well as third-party ones, with regular outside audits on how well it is working. The agreement also includes specific goals around false positive rates — that is, minors who are identified as over 18. And if a user is identified as under 13 and kicked off one of its platforms, Meta will check the ages of their friends, too. Face scans count as age assurance on some sites Identity verification companies like Yoti and Persona, which work with tech companies like Meta and Roblox, use video selfies people upload to estimate their ages. The gaming site Roblox, which, unlike social media platforms, allows kids under 13 to sign up, requires players to take a video selfie to estimate their age. Roblox says the videos are deleted after the age check is processed. Users are not required to submit a face scan to use the platform, only if they want to chat with other users. Some users have reported inaccuracies, and some experts have expressed caution about the reliability of facial age estimation tools, especially for women or certain racial or ethnic groups. But Matt Kaufman, chief safety officer at Roblox, said last year that for people between about 5 and 25, the system can accurately estimate their age within one or two years. Some websites and social media companies such as Meta have argued that age verification should be done by app store owners, such as Apple and Google, and not individual platforms. This would mean that app stores would have to verify their users’ ages before they allow them to download apps. Unsurprisingly, Apple and Google disagree. “Billed as ‘simple’ by its backers, including Meta, this proposal fails to cover desktop computers or other devices that are commonly shared within families. It also could be ineffective against pre-installed apps,” Google said in a blog post last year. Privacy concerns remain an obstacle Age checks are meant to keep kids out of online spaces that are not safe or appropriate for them, whether that’s social media or adult websites. But critics of online age verification see a worrisome trend toward a less secure, less private and less free internet, where people can be denied access not just to pornography but news, health information and the ability to speak openly and anonymously. What’s considered harmful to minors can be subjective, and this is where experts believe laws requiring age verification can run afoul of the First Amendment. The question could lead to people being required to verify their ages to access anything, from Netflix to a neighborhood blog. The digital rights group Electronic Frontier Foundation has been warning for years about “age-gating the internet.” “(No) matter the method, every system demands users hand over sensitive and immutable personal information that links their offline identity to their online activity,” EFF writes in a blog post. “Once that valuable data is collected, it can easily be leaked, hacked, or misused.”

headlines.title: California Legislature to vote on bill to aid wildfire victims after blocking parts of Newsom's plan
headlines.description: California lawmakers are expected to vote Tuesday on a bill aimed at supporting wildfire victims after rejecting an ambitious proposal by Gov. Gavin Newsom that would have limited electric companies’ financial liability for blazes sparked by their equipment. The Democratic governor said the last-minute compromise he made with lawmakers will have some benefits for wildfire victims, such as getting paid faster, but fails to make necessary, sweeping reforms to tackle the question of who covers the cost of fires ignited by utility equipment. His plan, which didn’t rack up enough support in the Legislature’s final days, would have reduced the amount utilities had to pay some victims and barred insurance companies from suing electrical companies to get reimbursed for damages paid out to homeowners. Newsom acknowledged the bill made some progress to address the contentious, high-stakes issue. “I could have easily walked away from it,” he told reporters at the Capitol on Monday. “And that would have been a disservice to you and the people of this state.” Who pays for wildfires is a contentious issue Newsom’s failure to get his full plan passed marked a rare loss for the governor, who has often found support for his policy wishes in the Democratic-led Legislature. It comes as he wraps his final session before leaving office in January. Fire victims heavily criticized his proposal, even protesting outside the governor’s mansion in Sacramento last week. They argued Newsom’s plan would have placed the needs of utilities over those of victims, while insurance companies said shifting more of the cost of damage onto them would have required them to raise rates for policyholders. Joy Chen, executive director of Every Fire Survivor’s Network, a group of victims of the 2025 Los Angeles-area fires, said the deal was a win for them. “Survivors from across California came to Sacramento and asked our elected representatives to stand with the people whose homes, communities and lives have been devastated,” she said in a statement. “They listened.” Newsom hoped his plan would help stabilize the state’s notoriously high electricity rates by protecting utilities from the full financial impacts of wildfires. Utilities have raised rates to pay for wildfire prevention and recovery as climate change has made the blazes more intense and frequent. Under California law, utilities have to pay damages for fires ignited by their equipment, even if a judge doesn’t find them negligent. The question of who should cover the cost of utility-sparked fires has persisted throughout Newsom’s tenure, which began after the most destructive wildfire in state history. He signed a law in 2019 — his first year in office — that created a $21 billion fund, paid for by utility shareholders and ratepayers, to help utilities pay for wildfire damages if they take certain safety measures. He and lawmakers agreed last year to supplement the pot of money with another $18 billion fund. Newsom unveiled his latest proposal as Southern California Edison faces claims from the state’s second-most destructive blaze, a 2025 fire that killed 19 people outside of Los Angeles. Compromise aims to pay victims faster The bill lawmakers are slated to vote on would create a program to ensure that fire victims get paid more quickly, ban hedge funds from profiting from wildfire claims and bar utility executives from receiving bonuses if their company’s equipment sparked a blaze that ends up damaging or destroying more than 500 buildings. The California Catastrophe Response Council, which oversees the wildfire fund, would appoint an administrator to create a process to resolve survivor claims more quickly. The American Property Casualty Insurance Association said the deal “protects Californians and preserves the affordability and availability of insurance.” “This outcome keeps costs with the parties responsible for wildfires and helps protect the progress California is making in stabilizing its insurance market,” the trade association wrote. Utilities and some lawmakers criticize the bill Pacific Gas & Electric, which filed for bankruptcy in 2019 after it faced claims from a devastating Northern California blaze started by the utility’s equipment, and Edison International, Southern California Edison’s parent company, were disappointed with the deal. They said in a letter to lawmakers that the bill would fail to stabilize rates for Californians and wouldn’t provide “durable, long-term solutions” for compensating victims, sustaining the state’s wildfire fund, or managing utilities’ financial risk. Assemblymember Rick Zbur, a Democrat, called it a “disaster” that lawmakers couldn’t agree on making more sweeping reforms. “We’re nibbling around the edges, and we’re not dealing with the structural issues,” he said at a hearing on the bill. Katelyn Roedner Sutter, of the Environmental Defense Fund, was also underwhelmed with the proposal, saying it wouldn’t go far enough to lower the risk of fires and stabilize electricity and insurance rates. “The best I can say about this bill is it’s fine,” she said after the hearing. The Legislature typically has until Aug. 31 to pass bills at the end of a two-year session, but lawmakers and Newsom couldn’t agree to a deal in time to vote Monday. They circumvented the end-of-session deadline by adding what’s known as an urgency clause to the bill. That means it needs approval from two-thirds of the Legislature and will take effect immediately after it’s signed into law. Legislature passes the nation’s first smoke contamination testing standards Lawmakers also passed a bill Monday that would create the nation’s first standards for testing and cleaning up lead, asbestos and other toxic contaminants inside homes after a wildfire. Assemblymember John Harabedian, a Democrat who wrote the bill, said it was borne out of the deadly 2025 Eaton Fire that swept through Altadena, which he represents. He said it’s important for lawmakers to “figure out very quickly how to protect wildfire survivors and rebuild communities,” and the bill is one way to do that. ___ Associated Press reporter Dorany Pineda in Los Angeles contributed to this report.

headlines.title: Suspect arrested in Richmond hit and run that left 81-year-old man dead
headlines.description: A suspect has been arrested one week after a hit and run killed a local 81-year-old family man, Richmond police said Monday. On Aug. 23 around 8:30 p.m., Rafael Gutierrez Delgado was struck by a car while crossing 23rd Street at Hellings Avenue in Richmond. The driver of the car continued to drive until Delgado was thrown from the hood, then fled the scene without stopping. The car was found abandoned in Richmond two days later. Don Mack, 66, a Richmond resident, was arrested on Sunday by police following a weeklong investigation that identified Mack as the alleged owner of an abandoned car connected to the fatal hit and run. Mack was arrested leaving an apartment on the 400 block of Fourth Street in Richmond and later booked into Contra Costa County Jail on suspicion of felony hit and run, vehicular manslaughter and driving with a suspended license, police said. Mack was known to police, who allege he has a “multiple-page rap sheet.” More than a dozen of Delgado’s family members and loved ones joined Richmond police for a press conference held at the department headquarters on Monday. “My dad didn’t deserve this,” said his daughter, Lucia Delgado. “He was very loved by his community. He always gave.” Delgado would have turned 82 on Tuesday. Lucia Delgado thanked local restaurants and neighbors for their outpouring of support and for the care packages sent to the family home. “The only thing I pray is that they feel in their conscience what we’re feeling in our grief,” Lucia said of Mack. “Senseless, horrible — two words that define this,” said Richmond Police Lt. Joseph England. “Mr. Delgado was well known. His community has gone through a lot in the last two weeks. This community is suffering,” he said, referring to a house fire killed a family of four in nearby central Richmond on Aug. 18. “What this family deserves, what this community deserves, that’s the most important thing for us,” he said. The hit and run is still under investigation, police said.

headlines.title: California lawmakers pass bill allowing people to identify their Jewish ancestry on state forms
headlines.description: California would allow Jews to voluntarily identify their Jewish heritage on state forms under a bill the state Legislature passed Monday. The bill, which lawmakers sent to Gov. Gavin Newsom’s desk, would require state agencies that collect demographic information to add “Jewish” as an option for ethnicity or ancestry. The goal is to give state officials and researchers better data on Jewish Californians, including their unemployment rates and representation in schools. The data would enable lawmakers to create policies that address the needs of Jews in the state, said David Bocarsly, CEO of Jewish California, an advocacy group. “It’s about inclusion as a community,” Bocarsly said, noting the Legislature has passed laws in recent years to collect more inclusive demographic data on Middle Eastern, North African and LGBTQ+ communities. Some opponents of the bill are worried about the idea of the state collecting such data given the traumatic history of the Nazi government keeping records of Jews during the Holocaust. The proposal would bar agencies from disclosing “personal identifying information,” and bill author Henry Stern, a Democratic state senator who is Jewish, said California already has robust privacy protections that should assuage those concerns. Sydney Levy of Jewish Voice for Peace, a progressive anti-Zionist group, wasn’t convinced by that argument. “When it comes to government holding lists of Jews, we do not trust your privacy guardrails,” Levy said at a hearing on the bill. Marc Dollinger, a Jewish studies professor at San Francisco State University, said in Jewish tradition, “Jews are not supposed to be counted.” “Ultimately, it becomes a question of trust: do California Jews have confidence that this form of data collection will support and protect them or will it elevate concerns over the possible harm this sort of counting can do?” he said in an email. Since the bill would categorize Jewish identity as an ethnicity, it could help the state track hate crimes against Jews, Dollinger said. Levy said he also disagrees with categorizing Jews as a single ethnic group. “Latino Jews like myself, as well as other Jews of color, have cultures and experiences different from those of white Jews,” Levy said at the hearing. Under the bill, people could still identify their race in addition to selecting “Jewish” for their ethnicity. It would be similar to how some people identify as Latino ethnically while describing their race as white, Native American or Black. The legislation was updated Friday to exempt agencies from adding “Jewish” as an option on their forms if they would for some reason lose federal funding for making the change. Stern started wearing a kippah to work in recent years, a sign of how his relationship to his Jewish identity has evolved throughout his life. On the same day that Hamas attacked Israel in October 2023, which launched the war in Gaza, Stern was walking to synagogue with his daughter, pushing her in a stroller, when people in a car went out of their way to yell an antisemitic remark at them, he said. Stern was wearing a kippah. He decided to wear it regularly after that. Stern said it was a big shift for someone who wasn’t very religious as a kid, though he would be reminded that he was different from other students in junior high school, when he was bullied for being Jewish. If Stern’s bill had been in place back then, it would have been a way to ensure his identity was better represented, he said. “This bill is just trying to create a little more space for those kinds of people — just let them be seen,” Stern said. “I don’t think it’s going to be a radical transformation. I don’t think it’s going to change the world.”

headlines.title: Immigrant rights advocates rally in SF in support of ‘No Kings Act'
headlines.description: Immigrant rights advocates are expected to rally in San Francisco on Tuesday in support of legislation that would allow people to file civil lawsuits against federal agents over alleged constitutional violations. Organizers point to a recent increase in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity and say the legislation would bring greater accountability to federal immigration enforcement. Senate Bill 747, known as the “No Kings Act,” was introduced in September 2025 by state Sen. Scott Wiener. The bill would allow people who claim they were mistreated or harmed by ICE agents to file lawsuits against the officers. The legislation recently passed both the California Senate and Assembly by comfortable margins and is now awaiting Gov. Gavin Newsom’s signature. The bill’s passage comes as reports of ICE activity and arrests have increased at airports, including San Francisco International Airport. Immigrant advocacy groups are expected to hold a rally and news conference Tuesday afternoon led by Wiener’s office and a man who says he survived an ICE raid. NBC Bay Area’s Ginger Conejero Saab has the full report in the video above.

headlines.title: Pedestrian struck, killed by driver in South San Jose
headlines.description: A pedestrian was struck and killed by a driver Monday night in South San Jose, according to police. The collision happened just after 8 p.m. near Vista Park Drive and Branham Lane, near Martial Cottle Park. Police have not identified the person who was killed. It was not immediately clear what led up to the collision. Police said the driver is cooperating with investigators. The investigation is ongoing.

headlines.title: Bicyclist struck, killed by vehicle in Hayward
headlines.description: A bicyclist was struck and killed by a car early Monday morning in Hayward, according to police. At about 12:10 a.m., officers were sent to the intersection of Harder and Soto roads on a report of a collision involving a vehicle and a bicyclist. According to investigators, a car being driven by a 52-year-old man from Hayward collided with a bicycle being ridden by a 62-year-old man. The driver of the car remained at the scene and cooperated. The bicyclist was taken to the hospital, where he was pronounced dead. His identity was withheld pending notification of next of kin and formal identification protocols by the Alameda County Coroner’s Office. It is not believed drugs or alcohol were factors in this collision, according to police. Anyone with information regarding this collision is asked to contact the Hayward Police Department Traffic Bureau at 510-293-7066.

headlines.title: Colin Kaepernick's unfinished business
headlines.description: Colin Kaepernick still puts in a workout at 4:30 a.m. most days. His football life may be long over, but his life’s work is not. Ten years after taking a knee to stand against racism and police brutality at great cost to his career and finances, the former star quarterback is stepping back into the spotlight. His memoir, “The Perilous Fight,” comes out on Sept. 15. And in interviews with NBC News, his first time speaking in depth about his protest’s fallout in years, Kaepernick reveals the story behind how he came to take a knee in 2016, an act that made him both a hero and a pariah, and one of the most divisive figures in the country. Kaepernick, 38, is now also a father to a 4-year-old girl. That, he says, helped him understand he has unfinished business in his life and cause. Being a dad “increases the responsibility and urgency of the work we’re doing,” he says. He doesn’t want his daughter — or anyone else — to think he stopped fighting or that the fight was not worth it.“I don’t want my community to watch me and have the takeaway be that if you fight for Black folks, it’s over for you,” he writes in his book. Much has shifted in American politics, culture, sports and policing since 2016. And much work still needs to be done, Kaepernick says, which is why he chose now to recount the decade-long odyssey that began with a quiet protest during the national anthem. Though the years have provided perspective, Kaepernick says they haven’t dulled his displeasure with the NFL. The quarterback who once led the San Francisco 49ers on a Disney movie-esque run to the Super Bowl in 2012 says he hasn’t watched an NFL game since he was exiled from the league. “I’m not gonna support an organization that one, is actively blackballing me, but two, has targeted my brothers who have been protesting as part of this as well,” Kaepernick says. “I watch college football.” (NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell has said on multiple occasions he doesn’t believe Kaepernick was blackballed.) On Sept. 1, 2016, Kaepernick and his San Francisco 49ers teammate Eric Reid took a knee during the national anthem before a preseason game. It was not the first time Kaepernick didn’t stand. His protest actually began a month earlier, on Aug. 14, when he sat on the bench during “The Star-Spangled Banner.” The idea had simmered in the months prior to the season when, he writes in his memoir, he was recuperating from surgeries. He might not have taken a knee if he hadn’t injured it first. The rehab gave him more free time than he ever had in his life. And in the midst of news of police violence, Kaepernick immersed himself in literature on Black liberation, reading books such as “The Autobiography of Malcolm X” and “Black Skin, White Masks” by Frantz Fanon. Eric Reid and Colin Kaepernick of the San Francisco 49ers kneel on the sideline during the national anthem prior to the game against the San Diego Chargers at Qualcomm Stadium on Sept. 1, 2016 in San Diego. Kaepernick says he hadn’t planned the initial protest in mid-August until he heard the opening of the anthem and felt he couldn’t bring himself to stand. No one seemed to notice him sitting at first. It wasn’t until after the 49ers’ third preseason game that Kaepernick was finally asked why he sat out the anthem. “I am not going to stand up to show pride in a flag for a country that oppresses Black people and people of color,” Kaepernick told NFL Network’s Steve Wyche. “To me, this is bigger than football and it would be selfish on my part to look the other way. There are bodies in the street and people getting paid leave and getting away with murder.” Kaepernick was unprepared for the response, he writes in the book. After the game, he called his partner, Nessa, and mentioned the reporter’s question. “Hmm. Well, what did you tell him?” she asked. “On a scale of one to 10, with 10 being the worst, how hard did you go?” “I don’t know. Maybe a four,” Kaepernick replied. The backlash was immediate. Fans burned his jerseys. Current and former players said he disrespected the flag. Donald Trump, then a presidential candidate, said Kaepernick “should find a country that works better for him.” “This is not a four, man,” Kaepernick recalls Nessa telling him when the news blew up. Even though the story of the protest has been told countless times since 2016, Kaepernick set the record straight on one key detail: who came up with the idea to kneel in the first place. Before the Sept. 1 game, Kaepernick was approached by Reid, who wanted to support the protest. It was Reid who suggested the idea to kneel, Kaepernick says. Not Army veteran Nate Boyer, as was widely reported at the time and since. Boyer, a Green Beret and former Seattle Seahawk, had penned an open letter to Kaepernick in the Army Times, writing: “Even though my initial reaction to your protest was one of anger, I’m trying to listen to what you’re saying and why you’re doing it.” On the day of the game, Boyer met with Kaepernick and Reid and relayed stories about how veterans responded to his open letter. The conversation, Boyer says, then shifted to how the protest could be respectful of the military. “I think it was Colin specifically that asked it. He said, ‘Well, do you think there’s a way that we could protest that’s not going to offend people in the military?’” Boyer recalls. “And I said, ‘No. No matter what, some people will be offended.’” Boyer then told Kaepernick he believed sitting on the bench “wasn’t the most inspiring” and that the protest could be more effective if he was next to his teammates, perhaps bowing his head while standing. “He said no immediately, and I respect that,” Boyer says, and the conversation then logically turned to taking a knee. He doesn’t dispute that the two players may have come to that conclusion before meeting him. “I remember them nodding their heads and looking at each other,” Boyer says. “Maybe Eric did suggest that, and that’s kind of what that look was.” After the Sept. 1 game, Reid told reporters “[Boyer] agreed with” the idea for them to kneel. Kaepernick says the notion it was Boyer’s idea appealed to the media because the backing of a white military veteran made the protest seem more “palatable.” As for why Kaepernick didn’t clear up the misconception at the time, he says he and Reid wanted to focus on their message, not get caught “in a personal back-and-forth over whose idea it was.” Though Kaepernick and Reid ultimately switched from sitting to kneeling, the protest continued to stoke controversy. Then-Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg called it “dumb and disrespectful.” Even Kaepernick’s adoptive parents initially said it was “disgraceful.” Along with the backlash, there was also a groundswell of support from the people he was protesting for, as well as athletes from other sports who joined the effort. “Oftentimes we hear a lot of the side of the pushback, but I think what’s disconnected from a lot of that is actually the response directly in communities that we were seeing, and the momentum and the excitement around the effort of no, we’re actually going to change this,” Kaepernick told NBC News during a recent sit-down. Those who condemned his protest chose to focus on his kneeling during the anthem — as opposed to the police violence that drove him to do it. “The critique of the method is a way to distract from the actual message,” Kaepernick says. “The conversation that was being had is taking a knee is more problematic than Black people being killed. Just simply put, ‘Hey, we need to talk about taking a knee. This is urgent. We need to resolve this.’ But another Black person gets killed, and it’s like, ‘Oh well, that’s kind of normal.’” In most of the coverage, Kaepernick’s assertion rang true. The conversation stuck to the red, white and blue, and not the disproportionate number of Black Americans killed by police that the quarterback tried to bring attention to. As Kaepernick tried desperately to keep his protest on message, the rest of his life was picked apart, from his romantic partner to his clothing choices. When Kaepernick revealed he didn’t vote in the 2016 election, ESPN’s Stephen A. Smith called him “irrelevant” and a “flaming hypocrite.” Reaction from players was also mixed. While Reid, Kaepernick and five other players kneeled in Week 1 of the 2016 season, many who said they were sympathetic to Kaepernick’s cause disagreed with his decision not to stand for the anthem. There was a group chat with roughly 100 players from all 32 teams that often grew contentious. In his memoir, Kaepernick writes of a text exchange in September 2016 in which then-Seahawks cornerback Richard Sherman told him he shouldn’t tell players how to protest. (Through his podcast producer, Sherman declined to comment.) The tension in the group chat was palpable, one former player in the chat who spoke on condition of anonymity tells NBC News. Some suggested Kaepernick was only kneeling for personal gain, even though by then it was clear he’d suffer a professional blow. In 2017, he became a free agent after the 49ers told him they would release him. The summer passed, and beyond a meeting with the Seattle Seahawks, no teams scheduled workouts. “I thoroughly enjoyed meeting with Colin, we just didn’t get to the next level,” then-Seahawks coach Pete Carroll wrote NBC News in an email about the meeting. Kaepernick says his meeting with Carroll and general manager John Schneider focused on his political beliefs. (The Seahawks did not respond to a request for comment.) “Which, in pretty much any environment outside the NFL, would be immediate litigation,” Kaepernick says. The same league that let Michael Vick play again after he went to prison for dogfighting, and allowed Deshaun Watson to sign a contract for $230 million following accusations of sexual misconduct by over 20 women (Watson has maintained his innocence), was keeping Kaepernick out. “There’s not a definitive moment that I would point to,” Kaepernick says about when he realized what was happening. Instead, it was more of a culmination. “Coming on the back of going to a Super Bowl, going to an NFC Championship, setting records, and not a single team would bring me in, even for a workout?” Kaepernick says. In August 2017, the Miami Dolphins — whose owner Stephen Ross previously launched a nonprofit to fight systemic racism — signed quarterback Jay Cutler after an injury to starter Ryan Tannehill, even though Cutler had already retired. NFL team executives, meanwhile, used the media to try to throw water on the idea that Kaepernick was blackballed. Some coaches and GMs did reach out, Kaepernick says, and explicitly told him, “Yeah, we want to bring you in, but it’s getting shut down above us.” One of those coaches, writes Kaepernick in his book, was John Harbaugh, the then-head coach of the Baltimore Ravens. Kaepernick spoke extensively with Harbaugh during the summer of 2017. Harbaugh’s brother Jim was Kaepernick’s coach during the 49ers’ run to the Super Bowl. Kaepernick writes that Harbaugh was “pushing” to sign him, but was “shut down from above.” In October 2017, Kaepernick filed a grievance against the NFL under the terms of the league’s and players’ collective bargaining agreement, alleging that owners were colluding against signing him due to his protest. “Everybody believes that he was blackballed,” says one former player who was in the league during 2016. “Players knew that this would happen. That was a firm belief around the league.” Goodell pushed back on the notion of organized collusion to keep Kaepernick out of the NFL. “Those are decisions that each individual owner has to make and their clubs, coaches, GMs,” Goodell told NBC in 2020. “And I’ve talked to a lot of our clubs about it and I’ve encouraged them. I’d love to see him play again.” In November 2019 — months after the NFL settled Kaepernick’s lawsuit — the league tried to arrange a midseason workout for him in front of all 32 teams. The details of this day are now infamous, as Kaepernick ultimately called off the NFL’s workout the morning of due to an extensive waiver he refused to sign — a waiver Kaepernick believed would sign away his employment rights and potential future claims — and instead managed to organize a workout of his own. The dissolution of the workout drew another round of skepticism, with many claiming Kaepernick was pulling a media stunt or was not serious about wanting to play again. While Kaepernick was out of the league, the NFL went about trying to turn the temperature down on his protest, battling the aftermath of an especially divisive election and a ratings slide some attributed to the player demonstrations. The league partnered in 2017 with the Players Coalition, a group founded to address systemic racism, and has since committed over half a billion dollars to various social justice causes. Kaepernick wasn’t part of the group. (Reid said in 2017 that Kaepernick was kicked out of communications with the group by co-founder Malcolm Jenkins, which Jenkins denied.) The NFL did whatever it could to stop the kneeling, the former player says, believing the league wanted to weed out players who kneeled: “What happened was the league and the Players Coalition came to a deal, and then the league did what they were going to do … They wanted their games to go back to normal.” Kaepernick’s protest likely cost him tens of millions of dollars, even accounting for whatever he got from the NFL in the settlement. But as his career was sacked, as television pundits continued to make personal attacks, and as 986 people were killed by police in 2017, Kaepernick stayed largely quiet. He says that was by design. “No individual should be speaking for everyone across the country. I don’t think that’s a responsible way to approach things,” Kaepernick says. “It’s also being able to enable other people to step into leadership positions, because that’s what movements actually are. It’s not one person just driving things.” Months after his workout snafu, events unrelated to Kaepernick raised the volume on his protest once more. On May 25, 2020, 46-year-old George Floyd was killed by police officer Derek Chauvin in Minnesota. Video revealed Chauvin kneeled on Floyd’s neck for over nine minutes, killing him. Chauvin was convicted on multiple murder charges in 2021. Nearly four years after Kaepernick kneeled in response to police brutality, worldwide protests emerged in the wake of Floyd’s killing. Kaepernick says seeing the protests around the world made him hopeful in the moment, especially as people in some cases risked their own well-being to be heard in the middle of the pandemic. “There was a significant portion of the population that previously was disconnected from these realities,” Kaepernick says. “It was like, oh, actually I have to sit with this now and I have to grapple with this. And am I OK with this? And what is my role within this? Am I complicit?” Corporations also scrambled to meet the moment, including the NFL. In June 2020, several NFL players coordinated social media posts asking for the league to condemn racism and “admit wrong in silencing our players from peacefully protesting.” The next day, Goodell responded in a video message. “We, the National Football League, condemn racism and the systematic oppression of Black people,” Goodell said in the video, echoing the words players demanded from him. “We, the National Football League, admit we were wrong for not listening to NFL players earlier and encourage all to speak out and peacefully protest. We, the National Football League, believe Black lives matter.” Kaepernick wasn’t impressed. “His response through that video was only because of pressure from players, not because it was altruistic,” Kaepernick says. The idea that the league should have listened to protesting players “is so laughable in my mind, and so disingenuous,” Kaepernick says. “We had been trying to address the issue that the NFL created with blackballing me for years. To come out and say we should have listened on the back of that — while I’m still actively trying to play in the NFL — it’s so performative.” Starting the season after Goodell’s video, the NFL began adding messages such as “Choose Love” and “End Racism” in the end zones of every stadium. It continued donating millions to the Inspire Change fund. In 2021, the league expanded on its Rooney Rule, which requires teams to interview at least two minority candidates for certain jobs. “‘End Racism’ in the back of the end zone is a great marketing campaign, but what are the actions behind it?” Kaepernick says. He adds that at the same time the league was putting slogans on the field, it was employing the practice of “race norming,” arguing that Black players began their careers with lower cognitive function in an effort to deny them payments as a result of a 2013 concussion lawsuit. (The NFL halted the practice in 2021.) “I don’t think the NFL has materially changed. None of their actions show that,” Kaepernick says. “We have seen it time and time again. For them it has gone back to business as usual, and I think that is a tragedy that we have allowed them to be able to get to that point.” In a statement to NBC News, the NFL said: “The issues Colin and other NFL players raised remain important to the league and deserving of continued attention and action,” noting the league still works with Inspire Change to “support meaningful progress.” The NFL added: “Since 2017, that work has reached thousands of national and grassroots partners, backed by more than $575 million in contributions. We remain committed to listening, collaborating, and taking action that creates lasting impact.” While 2020 appeared to cast Kaepernick’s protest in a more favorable light, the country’s collective backlash seemed even more pronounced after Trump was elected to a second term. Many corporations and college campuses rolled back their diversity, equality and inclusion practices. Many politicians disavowed or walked back their anti-police stances from the aftermath of Floyd’s death. Meanwhile, high-profile athletes, including some who supported Kaepernick, have retreated on taking political stances on issues such as the killing of Americans by immigration enforcement agents this year. “We have seen on the corporate side a shift in capitulation to the administration,” Kaepernick says, which he says in turn has had an effect on athletes. In this environment, Kaepernick says he tries to be strategic about when to speak up. “I try not to just flood things and be a stream of consciousness of everything because it does lose some of the impact,” he says. “I try to be intentional. When is it the right time and place for me to speak up on something?” Though his prospects of getting back on the field have dimmed, Kaepernick says he still trains as if he’s in the NFL. His daily routine typically begins with his early morning workout. Then, he says, his real work begins: He helps get his 4-year-old daughter ready for school. He devotes time to his various business endeavors, ranging from the Know Your Rights Camp to his AI company Lumi Story to his production house, Kaepernick Media. Being a father has especially added a new sense of urgency, he says. “You no longer have the luxury of thinking about it from a perspective of, it’s just me going through this world,” he says. “You think about it from the responsibility of creating an environment and a society that allows someone that is like your child to be able to grow up and thrive.” Kaepernick says his approach to politics has also evolved. He’s voted in the last two presidential elections and says he recognizes now that the strategy of not voting wasn’t right. Though still committed to his cause, Kaepernick says he often does his work behind the scenes. His Know Your Rights Camp has helped pay for 150 independent autopsies — such as the one for Nolan Wells this year — and has also paid hundreds of thousands in legal grants and bail relief. In August, Kaepernick pledged another $1 million to community organizations. Even as the country rubber-bands between the hyperactivism of 2020 and the cultural and political backlash since, Kaepernick — after all he’s been through — remains optimistic. “I’m very hopeful when I think about the moment that we are in,” Kaepernick says. Does that mean he feels his legacy is vindicated? “Candidly, I don’t think about legacy a whole lot,” he says. “What I think about is what are the areas that I can do work that I think are going to have an impact and help us move towards that future together. At the end of the day, people will decide what that legacy is, and hopefully that’s a positive one.”
